items.answer: So the browser kills playback first. The moment the voice detector hears you start talking, it flushes the audio queue and stops every scheduled source, so sound ends in under one hundred and fifty milliseconds with no server round trip. Then the server cancels the pipeline task, which propagates into the live model stream and synthesis jobs.

items.follow_up: So why did you not use it?
items.answer: Because it would hide the parts worth showing. A speech-to-speech model hears and speaks natively, so the vendor owns turn-taking and you never see where endpointing happens or what gets cancelled on an interrupt. This pipeline owns every one of those milliseconds, which is exactly what this deck is about.

items.question: Where does speech detection run?
items.answer: In your browser, not on a server. An audio worklet downmixes the mic, resamples to sixteen kilohertz, and measures loudness on every thirty-two millisecond frame, so nothing is streaming to a machine until you finish. That keeps interruption detection local, no round trip needed.

items.rationale: The answer accurately reflects the notes by stating that detection happens in the browser, describing the audio worklet's specific processing steps (downmixing, resampling to 16kHz, 32ms frames), and correctly noting that this keeps interruption detection local without a round trip.

items.question: What are the two tiers of interruption?
items.answer: Two tiers, actually. Tier one is the browser, which flushes playback the instant the voice detector hears you start talking, so sound stops in under one hundred and fifty milliseconds with no server round trip. Tier two is the server, which cancels the pipeline task and trims my history back to the sentences you actually heard, so I never think I said what I didn't.

suites.title: Latency

items.answer: It's about the system you're talking to right now. This deck walks through the whole voice agent pipeline, from how I hear you, to how I decide what to say, to how the audio comes back out. There's no speech-to-speech model in the middle. Your audio goes to Whisper for transcription, the text goes to an open-weight language model that answers and calls navigation tools, and my reply goes to Kokoro for speech. Every millisecond of that chain lives in this codebase, and the whole thing runs on open weights end to end.

items.answer: Two layers, actually. The browser stops the audio the instant it hears you speak, so the sound ends in under one hundred and fifty milliseconds with no server round trip. Then the server cancels the model and synthesis for that turn, and trims my history back to the sentences you actually heard, marked as interrupted by user. That trim is what stops me from believing I finished saying things you cut off.

items.id: Tell me about the latency budget.
items.answer: It comes down to milliseconds. From the moment you stop talking to the first sound I make, the budget is about one and a half seconds, with a ceiling of two and a half at the ninety-fifth percentile. Endpointing is the biggest chunk I actually control, at six hundred milliseconds of silence before I decide you are done.
